what_happened: The design job "Design Jev code-health checks as a shadow-mode design doc" was rejected at the final verdict. The verifier found one major problem: the design doc (docs/design/jev-code-health.md, sections 2, 7, 9 and 10, including J3 and J4) ignores the Jev client, fake and scoring code that already exists. Its build plan would rebuild that code, and its batching and cost assumptions are out of date. No acceptance criteria or failed checks were listed as unmet.
cause: Design jobs have no step that makes the producer inventory existing code, modules and fakes for the area before it proposes a build plan. Nothing compares the doc's proposed components against the repo, so a doc written from the request text or from memory looks complete. The gap surfaces only when the verifier reads the code at the end. The reading and planning stages also do not check the current repo state for such a job.
prevention: For design-type jobs, add a required "existing state" step before the producer drafts. The producer lists the existing modules, clients, fakes and tests for the area, with file paths. The design doc must carry an "Existing code" section, and every proposed build item must be marked new, extend or reuse against that list. The planning critic or a code check rejects a doc whose proposed components share a name or path with existing code but are marked new. Cost and batching assumptions must cite the existing code that determines them.
proposed_request: Revise docs/design/jev-code-health.md, the shadow-mode design for Jev code-health checks. First survey the repo for the Jev client, fake and scoring code that already exists, and add an "Existing code" section that lists each piece with its file path and what it does. Then rewrite the build plan (sections 2, 7, 9 and 10, including J3 and J4) so each item is marked reuse, extend or new. Do not rebuild anything that exists. Update the batching and cost assumptions to match how the existing client and scoring code actually work, and cite the code. Change only the design doc. It is done when every build item is checked against the survey, no item duplicates existing code, and the batching and cost figures agree with the current code.
